title: I Enforced the Pottery-Wheel Timer on the Resident Whose Intern Camped My Bat

parts.text: I stepped into wheel six at 2:05 p.m. and resident Ines was already using my numbered bat. The board said: NINETY MINUTES. BATS STAY WITH THE WHEEL. I was twenty-eight, clay-studio lead, holding a sign-up that listed our block. Ines shrugged. "Residents own the wheel." I photographed the board, the booking, and her intern throwing on my bat. Then I asked for the wheel timer. At 2:13 the studio desk pinged why Ines's intern was on wheel six. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The studio desk can see an intern throwing on wheel six during our block.

social.video_title: Her intern camped my numbered bat — Part 1/2
social.description: Pottery studio, an intern on my bat, a ninety-minute clock she posted. I logged the throw. Would you have asked for the wheel timer?

parts.text: Ines called it centering practice until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the wheel still. The bat went back to my numbered stack. Ines ran a slot of their own and told the next resident atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: RESIDENTS DO NOT OWN THE WHEEL. I keep our block on a labeled card. Ines brown-bags intern hours. The wheel finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Residents do not own the wheel — Part 2/2
social.description: Wheel timer, numbered bat, and a second line on the board. Was centering ever our block?
